title: AAST terminology gap supplement — hypersomnolence, EEG, electrode placement, and professional context
sourceRole: Learner-ready Sleep Pathways Guild definitions for high-value AAST inventory gaps spanning hypersomnolence, EEG/neurologic recognition, electrode placement, respiratory/PAP context, and professional terminology.
apaReference: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
copyrightBoundary: Term names and abbreviations are factual inventory data. Definitions and memory clues in this file are original Sleep Pathways Guild summaries and do not reproduce published AAST, AASM, ICSD, textbook, or atlas definitions.
reviewFocus: Central disorders of hypersomnolence, sleep-wake neurobiology, EEG/neurologic recognition, electrode placement, bilevel pressure ranges, and selected professional-practice terms.

items.definition: A professional medical society in sleep medicine whose publications include sleep-scoring standards, clinical practice guidance, accreditation standards, and the International Classification of Sleep Disorders.
items.memoryClue: AASM = scoring standards, clinical guidance, accreditation, and ICSD.

items.definition: A professional association focused on education, practice resources, and professional development for sleep technologists and other sleep-technology professionals.
items.memoryClue: AAST = professional association for sleep technologists.

items.definition: A credentialing organization for sleep technologists that administers credentials including the Registered Polysomnographic Technologist and Certified Polysomnographic Technician credentials.
items.memoryClue: BRPT = the credentialing body behind RPSGT and CPSGT.

items.definition: A credit used to document participation in approved continuing-education activity; credentialing or licensing programs may require specified continuing-education credits for renewal.
items.memoryClue: CEC = documented continuing professional education.

items.term: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
items.definition: A United States federal law and related rules that establish national requirements for privacy, security, and appropriate handling of identifiable health information in healthcare settings.
items.memoryClue: HIPAA = protect identifiable health information.

items.definition: A condition in which gastric contents repeatedly reflux into the esophagus and cause troublesome symptoms or complications; symptoms may occur or worsen during the night.
items.memoryClue: GERD = stomach contents reflux into the esophagus.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: The unit of frequency equal to one cycle per second. PSG waveform frequencies and many filter settings are expressed in hertz.
items.memoryClue: 1 Hz = 1 cycle each second.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: A hypothalamic neuropeptide system, also called orexin, that helps stabilize wakefulness. Markedly reduced hypocretin signaling is strongly associated with narcolepsy type 1.
items.memoryClue: Hypocretin/orexin helps hold wakefulness steady.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine. (2023). International classification of sleep disorders (3rd ed., text rev.). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A brain region that integrates sleep-wake regulation with circadian, autonomic, endocrine, temperature, and behavioral control; it includes the suprachiasmatic nucleus and wake-promoting orexin neurons.
items.memoryClue: Hypothalamus = circadian control plus sleep-wake regulation.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: A central disorder of hypersomnolence characterized by persistent excessive sleepiness that is not adequately explained by another sleep, medical, neurologic, psychiatric, medication, or substance cause and does not meet the defining pattern for narcolepsy.
items.memoryClue: Idiopathic hypersomnia = persistent central sleepiness without the defining narcolepsy pattern.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine. (2023). International classification of sleep disorders (3rd ed., text rev.). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: A sleep complaint involving difficulty initiating sleep, maintaining sleep, or waking earlier than desired with associated daytime consequences despite adequate opportunity and circumstances for sleep.
items.memoryClue: Insomnia = difficulty sleeping plus daytime impact despite opportunity for sleep.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine. (2023). International classification of sleep disorders (3rd ed., text rev.). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: The portion of the respiratory cycle during which airflow moves into the lungs. In bilevel PAP, the inspiratory phase is the phase associated with the inspiratory positive airway pressure setting.
items.memoryClue: Inspiratory phase = air moving in; bilevel uses IPAP here.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: The lowest inspiratory positive airway pressure that a variable bilevel or servo-ventilation mode is permitted to deliver within its configured inspiratory-pressure range; the exact behavior depends on the device and mode.
items.memoryClue: IPAP min = lower boundary of allowed inspiratory pressure.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: The highest inspiratory positive airway pressure that a variable bilevel or servo-ventilation mode is permitted to deliver within its configured inspiratory-pressure range; the exact behavior depends on the device and mode.
items.memoryClue: IPAP max = upper boundary of allowed inspiratory pressure.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: A standardized method for locating scalp EEG electrodes by measuring proportional distances between defined head landmarks, creating reproducible electrode positions across patients.
items.memoryClue: 10-20 = proportional head measurements for reproducible EEG locations.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.

Troester, M. M., Quan, S. F., Berry, R. B., et al. (2023). The AASM manual for the scoring of sleep and associated events: Rules, terminology and technical specifications (Version 3). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine diagnostic classification system that organizes sleep disorders into recognized categories and provides diagnostic criteria and terminology; the current text revision is ICSD-3-TR.
items.memoryClue: ICSD = AASM diagnostic classification; current text revision is ICSD-3-TR.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
American Academy of Sleep Medicine. (2023). International classification of sleep disorders (3rd ed., text rev.). American Academy of Sleep Medicine.

items.definition: Rhythms arising from the atrioventricular junction rather than the sinoatrial node. P waves may be absent, inverted, or retrograde, while the QRS is often narrow unless conduction is abnormal.
items.memoryClue: Junctional rhythm = AV junction takes over the pacemaker role.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: A rare childhood epileptic encephalopathy associated with acquired loss or regression of language skills and epileptiform EEG abnormalities that are often more prominent during sleep.
items.memoryClue: Landau-Kleffner = acquired language regression plus sleep-activated epileptiform EEG.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Attarian, H. P., & Morgan, M. Y. (Eds.). (2012). Atlas of electroencephalography in sleep medicine. Springer.

items.definition: A severe childhood epileptic encephalopathy characterized by multiple seizure types, cognitive impairment, and characteristic EEG abnormalities; sleep can increase or reveal epileptiform activity.
items.memoryClue: Lennox-Gastaut = multiple seizure types with characteristic abnormal EEG.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Attarian, H. P., & Morgan, M. Y. (Eds.). (2012). Atlas of electroencephalography in sleep medicine. Springer.

items.definition: A major jaw-closing muscle. Surface EMG from the masseter can be used in selected sleep recordings to help characterize jaw-muscle activity such as sleep-related bruxism.
items.memoryClue: Masseter closes the jaw; its EMG can track jaw-muscle activity.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Robertson, B., Marshall, B., & Carno, M.-A. (2014). Polysomnography for the sleep technologist: Instrumentation, monitoring, and related procedures. Mosby.

items.definition: A normal wake EEG rhythm over the central sensorimotor regions, commonly in the alpha-frequency range, that is reduced by movement or movement intention and can be distinguished from posterior alpha by location and reactivity.
items.memoryClue: Mu = central sensorimotor rhythm that blocks with movement.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Attarian, H. P., & Morgan, M. Y. (Eds.). (2012). Atlas of electroencephalography in sleep medicine. Springer.

items.definition: A sudden, brief, involuntary muscle jerk caused by a short burst of muscle activity or a brief interruption of ongoing muscle activity. Myoclonus is a broad movement phenomenon and is not synonymous with periodic limb movements of sleep.
items.memoryClue: Myoclonus = sudden brief jerk; PLMS is a specific periodic sleep pattern.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
Attarian, H. P., & Morgan, M. Y. (Eds.). (2012). Atlas of electroencephalography in sleep medicine. Springer.

items.definition: A central disorder of hypersomnolence marked by persistent excessive sleepiness and dysregulation of REM sleep. Current classification distinguishes narcolepsy type 1 from type 2 using clinical and biologic criteria defined by ICSD-3-TR.
items.memoryClue: Narcolepsy = chronic sleepiness plus REM dysregulation; ICSD separates type 1 and type 2.
references: American Association of Sleep Technologists. (2016). Sleep technology terms and definitions (2nd ed.). American Association of Sleep Technologists.
